name: Oak Island Money Pit
description: Oak Island is a 57-hectare (140-acre) tree-covered island in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, the focus of one of the longest-running treasure hunts in history. Since 1795, expeditions have excavated the so-called 'Money Pit' in search of buried treasure, with multiple deaths but no verified treasure recovered.
full_description: Oak Island is one of the roughly 360 small islands in Mahone Bay on the south shore of Nova Scotia, Canada. According to the standard account, in the summer of 1795 a teenager named Daniel McGinnis discovered a circular depression in the ground beneath an old oak tree, with evidence of a block-and-tackle in the branches above. With friends John Smith and Anthony Vaughan, he began excavating and reportedly found layers of flagstones and oak log platforms at roughly 3-metre (10-foot) intervals, abandoning the dig at about 9 metres (30 feet). Subsequent expeditions — the Onslow Company (c. 1804), the Truro Company (1849), the Oak Island Association (1861) and many others — encountered repeated flooding once shafts passed about 27 metres (90 feet), allegedly caused by elaborate flood-tunnel booby-traps connected to nearby Smith's Cove. Six men have died on the island during excavations, including a worker killed in 1861 when a steam-engine boiler burst, Maynard Kaiser in 1897, and four men (Robert Restall, Robert Restall Jr., Karl Graeser and Cyril Hiltz) in 1965 from hydrogen-sulfide gas exposure. Notable purported finds include coconut fibre (anomalous for Nova Scotia), a small parchment fragment with the letters 'vi' or 'wi' (1897), and a since-lost stone slab said to bear ciphered text recovered from the pit. From 1965 the Triton Alliance (Daniel Blankenship and David Tobias) operated the major modern excavation; from 2006 onward Michigan brothers Rick and Marty Lagina acquired a controlling interest in Oak Island Tours Inc., and in 2014 the History Channel began the long-running reality series The Curse of Oak Island. Mainstream historians, including geologist Robert Dunfield's findings, archivist Joy Steele, and folklorist Richard Joltes, argue that almost all 'engineered' features can be explained by natural sinkhole geology in the local anhydrite/gypsum bedrock combined with later excavation disturbance and the 19th-century mythologising of the McGinnis story; many of the apparently early reports first appear in newspapers from the 1860s. Despite over 230 years of effort, no treasure has been verifiably recovered.
origin: A single island in Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, Canada, accessed from the village of Western Shore by a causeway constructed in 1965.

etymology.origin: English; named for the red oak (Quercus rubra) trees historically growing on the island, which inspired the original 1795 name 'Oak Island'. The term 'Money Pit' was applied by 19th-century newspapers describing the central excavation.
etymology.meaning: Oak Island = 'island of oaks'; Money Pit = the central excavation believed to conceal buried treasure.
etymology.first_use: 'Oak Island' attested in late-18th-century Nova Scotia maps; 'Money Pit' popularised in mid-19th-century treasure-hunt journalism.

timeline.event: Daniel McGinnis, John Smith and Anthony Vaughan reportedly discover a depression and oak-log platforms on Oak Island; abandon the dig at about 9 m (30 ft)
timeline.source: Wikipedia, 'Oak Island mystery'; later 19th-century newspaper accounts

timeline.event: The Onslow Company excavates to about 27 m (90 ft) before the pit floods with seawater
timeline.significance: Establishes the 'flooding' phenomenon central to the mystery

timeline.event: The Truro Company resumes excavation and reportedly recovers wooden platforms and metal in pieces from boring
First confirmed death on the island when a steam-engine boiler bursts during excavation
Worker Maynard Kaiser dies in a fall during excavation; later that year a small piece of parchment with letters 'vi' or 'wi' is reportedly brought up from depth
Future U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt invests in the Old Gold Salvage and Wrecking Company excavation
Robert Restall, his son Robert Jr., Karl Graeser and Cyril Hiltz die from hydrogen sulfide gas exposure in a shaft on Smith's Cove
timeline.significance: Worst single incident on the island; four deaths in one day

timeline.event: Geologist Robert Dunfield bulldozes large areas of the eastern end of the island; argues for natural-sinkhole explanation
Daniel Blankenship and David Tobias form the Triton Alliance and acquire excavation rights
timeline.significance: Begins the principal modern excavation era

timeline.event: Triton Alliance sinks Borehole 10-X; underwater camera footage allegedly shows tools and a severed hand (interpretation disputed)
Michigan brothers Rick and Marty Lagina acquire a 50% interest in Oak Island Tours Inc.
timeline.significance: Sets up the modern television era

timeline.event: History Channel premieres 'The Curse of Oak Island', following the Lagina-led excavation

cultural_notes: Local belief alternates between treating the island as a genuine engineering and treasure mystery and as a long-running cautionary tale about ruinous obsession.
